lesson.title: When Nothing You Do Seems to Matter
lesson.summary: Learned helplessness is the passive, give-up response that develops after repeated exposure to uncontrollable negative events, and it became one of psychology's most influential models of depression.
lesson.body:
Operant conditioning assumes that behavior is shaped by its consequences: responses that are reinforced increase, and responses followed by punishment decrease. But what happens when punishment or discomfort arrives no matter what an organism does, when there is no response that changes the outcome at all? Martin Seligman and Steven Maier's research in the late 1960s gave a surprising and influential answer.

In the original studies, dogs were placed in a harness and exposed to electric shocks they could not escape or avoid no matter what they did, a kind of inescapable positive punishment with no available response to stop it. A second group of dogs received shocks they could escape by a simple action, and a third group received no shocks at all. Later, all the dogs were placed in a shuttle box, a chamber divided by a low barrier, where jumping over the barrier during a shock would successfully escape it, a task most dogs learn quickly. The dogs that had previously experienced escapable shock, or no shock, learned to jump the barrier without much trouble. But many of the dogs that had previously experienced inescapable shock simply lay down and passively endured the shocks, making little or no attempt to escape, even though escape was now completely possible.

Seligman and Maier's interpretation was that the dogs from the inescapable-shock group had learned, from their earlier experience, that their behavior had no effect on what happened to them, and they carried that expectation into a brand-new situation where it no longer applied. This is learned helplessness: a learned expectation of futility that generalizes beyond the original uncontrollable situation and suppresses attempts to act, even when acting would actually work.

The concept became enormously influential as a model for human depression. People who face repeated, uncontrollable failure or adversity can develop a similar pattern: passivity, low motivation, and a sense that effort is pointless, even once their circumstances change and effective action becomes available again. Later researchers, including Seligman himself, refined the theory by adding explanatory style, the particular way a person habitually explains bad events to themselves, as a key factor in who becomes helpless and who doesn't; that refinement connects directly to attribution theory, covered later in this unit. It's also worth noting that some later work, including further research by Seligman and colleagues, has revisited and nuanced parts of the original account, so the theory is best understood as a highly influential starting point rather than a final, settled explanation of passivity and depression.
